Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

at the house of preposition

also at someone’s house, at my place, at someone’s place

classical

Catull. 13.1: cēnābis bene, mī Fabulle, apud mē
Plaut. Aul. 243: hīc apud mē hortum cōnfodere jussī

apud (+ accusative)

preposition with the accusative

at the house of, with (a person)

With a person, at their home: apud mē, at my house; apud avum, at Grandpa’s. Also in someone’s presence (apud jūdicem), and among a people (see among).

Other words

  • ad (+ accusative) — to the house of (going there)

    preposition with the accusative · also used · classical · Cic. Att. 4.4a.1: perbellē fēceris sī ad nōs vēneris

    With verbs of motion: ad mē venī, come to my house; ad avum īmus, we are going to Grandpa’s.

  • domī (+ genitive or a possessive) — at the house of

    locative of domus · also used · classical · Cic. Att. 1.12.3: dēprehēnsum domī C. Caesaris

    Domī meae, at my house; domī Caesaris, at Caesar’s house. Going there, domum meam.

Examples

  • cēnābis bene, mī Fabulle, apud mē paucīs, sī tibi dī favent, diēbus

    you will dine well at my house, my Fabullus, in a few days, if the gods are kind to youCatull. 13.1–2

  • Hīc apud mē hortum cōnfodere jussī.

    I’ve had the garden dug over here at my place.Plaut. Aul. 243

  • perbellē fēceris sī ad nōs vēneris

    it would be lovely of you to come to usCic. Att. 4.4a.1

  • P. Clōdium Appī f., crēdō tē audīsse cum veste muliebrī dēprehēnsum domī C. Caesaris

    I expect you have heard that Publius Clodius, son of Appius, was caught in women’s clothes at Gaius Caesar’s houseCic. Att. 1.12.3

  • Hodiē apud avum cēnābimus.

    Today we’re having dinner at Grandpa’s.composed

See also at, to, house, among.
